steps.tx: Rare, life-threatening chromaffin cell neuroendocrine tumours originating in the adrenal medulla synthesize, store, and episodically release excessive catecholamines. Clinically designated as a **phaeochromocytoma**, this tumour produces paroxysmal or sustained severe hypertension accompanied by the classic clinical triad: episodic pounding headache, profuse generalized diaphoresis, and sudden palpitations or tachycardia. Paroxysms occur abruptly and last minutes to hours, provoked by physical exertion, postural changes, abdominal palpation, micturition, or medications including beta-blockers and metoclopramide. Untreated catecholamine storms risk fatal hypertensive encephalopathy, aortic dissection, myocardial infarction, and stress-induced cardiomyopathy (Takotsubo syndrome).

steps.tx: Biochemical confirmation of catecholamine excess relies on detecting stable methylated metabolites rather than fleeting parent catecholamine molecules. Measuring free **plasma metanephrines** (metanephrine and normetanephrine) represents the single most sensitive initial diagnostic screening test, exceeding ninety-seven percent sensitivity. Within chromaffin tumour cells, catecholamines are continuously metabolized into metanephrines by membrane-bound catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT), independently of exocytotic catecholamine release. Blood must be drawn in a supine resting state after twenty minutes of cannulation to prevent false-positive adrenergic surges, with elevations greater than three times the upper reference limit virtually establishing the diagnosis.

steps.tx: Twenty-four-hour urinary collections provide essential corroboration and remain valuable alternatives when plasma assays are equivocal. Measuring urinary fractionated metanephrines and **vanillylmandelic acid** (VMA) quantifies daily total catecholamine metabolite excretion. Vanillylmandelic acid, the stable final end-product of catecholamine degradation, exhibits high diagnostic specificity but lower sensitivity (roughly seventy-five percent) compared to metanephrines. Patients must adhere to strict dietary restrictions during urine collection, avoiding coffee, tea, chocolate, bananas, and citrus fruits, alongside pausing sympathomimetic decongestants, labetalol, and tricyclic antidepressants to prevent spurious laboratory elevations.

steps.tx: Once biochemical hypersecretion is confirmed, anatomical and functional imaging localizes the primary tumour and detects occult metastases. High-resolution non-contrast computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging of the abdomen and pelvis localizes greater than ninety-five percent of tumours. Phaeochromocytomas appear as large, vascular, heterogeneous adrenal masses with prominent cystic or necrotic components. For functional localization, whole-body nuclear scintigraphy using an **mibg scan** (iodine-123 metaiodobenzylguanidine) concentrates selectively in adrenergic chromaffin vesicles via the norepinephrine transporter, identifying extra-adrenal paragangliomas, multiple tumours in genetic syndromes, and metastatic bone deposits.

steps.tx: Rigorous, sequential pharmacological adrenergic receptor blockade is mandatory prior to surgical extirpation to avert intraoperative catastrophe. Initiating oral **phenoxybenzamine**, an irreversible, non-competitive alpha-adrenergic receptor antagonist, begins ten to fourteen days before surgery. It prevents lethal intraoperative hypertensive crises during tumour manipulation and enables vascular volume expansion, because chronic intense alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction severely contracts plasma volume. Patients are instructed to consume high-sodium diets and liberal fluid intake. Beta-adrenergic antagonists (such as propranolol or metoprolol) may only be added several days AFTER complete alpha-blockade to control reflex tachycardia.

Controls reflex tachycardia; never give as monotherapy
Confirms adequate safe preoperative haemodynamic blockade

steps.tx: Administering a beta-adrenergic receptor antagonist prior to establishing complete alpha-adrenergic receptor blockade carries disastrous clinical consequences. If a beta-blocker is mistakenly administered alone, blockade of vasodilatory vascular beta-2 receptors leaves catecholamine-mediated alpha-1 vasoconstriction completely unopposed. This trigger precipitates catastrophic, refractory **hypertensive crisis**, acute coronary vasospasm, acute pulmonary oedema, and intracranial haemorrhage. Therefore, clinical guidelines strictly enforce the ironclad axiom: alpha-blockade must ALWAYS precede beta-blockade by several days, ensuring safe adrenergic suppression before general anaesthesia.

steps.tx: Laparoscopic transperitoneal or retroperitoneal adrenalectomy constitutes the definitive curative therapy for adrenal phaeochromocytoma. During surgical resection, gentle dissection and early ligation of the main adrenal vein prevent intraoperative surges of catecholamines into the systemic circulation. Following tumour excision, sudden withdrawal of high circulating catecholamines combined with persistent irreversible alpha-blockade frequently triggers profound, life-threatening postoperative **hypotension**. Management requires aggressive intraoperative volume loading with isotonic crystalloids and temporary vasopressor support with norepinephrine until vascular tone recovers.

steps.tx: Roughly thirty to forty percent of all phaeochromocytomas arise in the setting of hereditary cancer predisposition syndromes. Germline mutations in RET (MEN 2A/2B), VHL (von Hippel-Lindau disease), NF1 (neurofibromatosis type 1), and SDHD/SDHB (succinate dehydrogenase subunits) drive familial disease. Because clinical malignancy cannot be diagnosed histologically and is defined strictly by the presence of metastases in non-chromaffin tissues (bones, lymph nodes, liver), every patient with phaeochromocytoma requires lifetime annual biochemical surveillance with plasma **metanephrine surveillance**.
